title: Welcome to “Un timp al lor”
subtitle: For curious people and for those who dream: what science knows, what it does not know yet, and where the dream ends
body_html:
Versiunea în limba română: Bun venit la „Un timp al lor”.

The launch post of “Un timp al lor” (Romanian for “A time of their own”), first published in Romanian on 29 October 2026. The blog is written in Romanian; each text now also has an English version.

There are many questions about artificial intelligence, about mind, memory and time, that trouble me and that, I have seen, trouble others too. The answers you usually find are of two kinds: either too technical to follow, or too loud to believe. Between them there is an empty space. I am trying to fill it here.

“Un timp al lor” sets out to be a place for popular science, in Romanian, written for curious people, because I am one too. And for people who dream. All science starts this way: someone looks at an ordinary thing and imagines what might lie beyond it. The dream shows where to look; science checks what is true. Here I stand on the threshold between the two, and try to understand, each time, where the dream ends and where the result begins.

I am convinced of one thing: if you are curious enough to have dreams of your own, this road is open to you as well. The door between dreaming and science opens for anyone patient enough to push it. This page is, in the end, an invitation to study: from dreaming towards the world of science.

The title is a small invitation to imagination. “Un timp al lor”, a time of their own, is the time that minds made of computation would measure if they had a clock of their own. Literally, it is the question I start from: how could an agent keep track of its own change, of its own “mileage”, without depending on a clock outside itself? More broadly, it is our times, in which artificial intelligence is already part of everyday life as a powerful working tool, and in which part of the effort to develop it aims to turn it, gradually, into a partner of humans, in work and in thought. A partner, however, has to be trustworthy, and trust rests on evidence, not on impressions. That is where my questions start.

What I set out to do. To tell, in accessible terms, what real research looks like: with its precise questions, its modest results, its dead ends and its corrections. Where something is not known, I will say “it is not known”. Where I was wrong, I will say that too. I do not promise definitive answers and I do not claim to hold the only point of view; I offer a documented perspective, with sources that can be checked.

Where I start from. The first series, five texts, starts from two papers I have written and published in open access on Zenodo: a theoretical one, on how an agent’s time might be understood, and a first experiment, which ended with a practically null result. A second experiment is still at the protocol stage and has no results. The papers are published without formal editorial review, so I present them as what they are: a documented perspective and an honest test, not verdicts. I drafted and checked them with the help of artificial intelligence assistants; responsibility for the content is mine. This is a personal, independent undertaking, with no claim to change a field. I will be glad if it leaves good questions behind, which may give rise to other ideas, mine or yours.

What you get. One text on Tuesday mornings. The first, “An agent that wakes up”, is already published; the next ones appear on 3, 10, 17 and 24 November. If there is interest, I will continue with other series. The scientific papers behind the texts are public, in open access, on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23671714

If you find it interesting, I invite you to subscribe. Comments are open to subscribers, and questions and objections are welcome.
